segments.text: Sociological theory provides different lenses for explaining social order, inequality, meaning and change. The syllabus requires three broad perspectives—structural functionalism, symbolic interaction and conflict—plus major thinkers from Ibn Khaldun to Talcott Parsons.
The easiest method is not biography. For each thinker learn: central question → core concepts → view of society/change → one application → one criticism.

items.text: Structural functionalism

: Functionalism views society as a system of interdependent parts and asks how institutions contribute to order, continuity or adaptation. It is useful for explaining integration but can understate conflict and inequality.
Symbolic interaction

: Symbolic interaction focuses on face-to-face interaction, meanings, symbols and how social reality is constructed in everyday life. It is strong at the micro level but may give less attention to large structures.
Conflict perspective
: Conflict approaches emphasize unequal resources, power and competing interests. They explain inequality and change well but can sometimes understate cooperation and shared values.
Ibn Khaldun

: Ibn Khaldun analysed social organization, political authority and historical change. His concept of asabiyyah—group solidarity or social cohesion—is central to his explanation of the rise and decline of political groups.
Auguste Comte

: Comte helped establish sociology as a distinct discipline and promoted positivism, the idea that society could be studied systematically. His “law of three stages” is historically important but should not be treated as a proven universal law.
Herbert Spencer

: Spencer used evolutionary and organismic analogies to explain social differentiation and interdependence. His work influenced early sociology but some evolutionary claims are now heavily criticized.
Émile Durkheim
: Durkheim emphasized social facts, division of labour, solidarity, anomie and the social causes of suicide. He demonstrated how apparently individual behaviour can show social patterns.
Karl Marx
: Marx analysed class relations, modes of production, exploitation, alienation and conflict. He saw material/economic relations as central to historical change.
Max Weber
: Weber emphasized social action, meaning, authority, bureaucracy, rationalization and the role of ideas as well as material interests. His interpretive approach complements structural explanations.
Talcott Parsons

: Parsons developed a systems approach emphasizing social order, roles, values and functional requirements. His theory is influential but often criticized for abstraction and insufficient attention to conflict.
Comparative understanding

: Durkheim asks how social order/integration is maintained; Marx emphasizes class and material conflict; Weber combines meaning, authority, ideas and institutions. Comparing them is more useful than memorizing quotations.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

A sociological theory identifies important social mechanisms and organizes evidence around a question: how is order maintained, why does inequality persist, how do meanings shape action, or how do societies change? Theories are not lists of quotations. They are connected arguments with assumptions, concepts and implications.

items.text: Macro and micro
: Macro theories focus on institutions, classes, states and large-scale structures; micro theories examine interaction, identity and meaning. The levels are different rather than mutually exclusive.
Structure and agency

: Some theories emphasize structural constraints while others emphasize action and interpretation. Strong sociological analysis often asks how structures shape choices and how repeated choices reproduce or transform structures.
Central idea
: Society is viewed as a system of interdependent institutions whose patterned activities contribute to continuity, adaptation and coordination.
Durkheimian foundation
: Durkheim's analysis of solidarity and social facts influenced later functionalism by showing how institutions and norms exist beyond any one individual and support social integration.
Parsons

: Parsons developed a highly abstract systems theory in which action is organized through shared values and differentiated institutional functions. His AGIL scheme described adaptation, goal attainment, integration and latency/pattern maintenance as functional requirements of systems.
Merton's refinement
: Robert K. Merton distinguished manifest from latent functions and introduced dysfunctions. This made functional analysis less dependent on assuming that every institution benefits everyone.
Criticism
: Functionalism can overstate consensus, treat existing institutions as necessary and underplay coercion, inequality and rapid change. A function for one group can be a dysfunction for another.
Meaning
: People act toward objects, roles and others based on meanings, and those meanings emerge through interaction.
Mead
: Mead explained the self through role-taking, the 'I' and 'Me', and the generalized other. The self is social because people learn to view themselves from others' perspectives.
Blumer
: Herbert Blumer named symbolic interactionism and emphasized that meanings are interpreted rather than mechanically transmitted.
Goffman
: Goffman's dramaturgical approach analyzes how people manage impressions in different settings, using concepts such as front stage and back stage.
Criticism
: Interactionism provides rich accounts of everyday life but can understate how class, law and institutions constrain the very situations in which meanings are negotiated.
Central idea
: Society contains groups with unequal resources and interests. Institutions can stabilize cooperation while also reproducing domination.
Marx
: Marx located major conflict in relations of production, especially between owners of productive property and wage labour. Class structure, exploitation and accumulation shape politics and ideas.
Beyond economic class

: Later conflict approaches examine gender, race, ethnicity, state power and organizations. These extensions should be linked to specific mechanisms rather than turning 'conflict' into a generic word for disagreement.
Criticism
: Conflict theories can understate shared values, routine cooperation and the autonomy of culture when every institution is explained only as domination.
Context

: Writing in the fourteenth century, Ibn Khaldun sought systematic explanations of political rise and decline in the Muqaddimah. He compared modes of livelihood, group organization, authority and historical change.
Asabiyyah

: Asabiyyah refers to group solidarity or social cohesion that enables collective action. Strong solidarity can support political expansion, while success and settled luxury may weaken the cohesion that originally sustained a ruling group.
Bedouin-sedentary contrast
: Ibn Khaldun contrasted relatively austere tribal/pastoral groups with settled urban dynasties. The model is historical and cyclical, not a timeless law applying identically to every state.
Method

: He criticized uncritical transmission of historical reports and emphasized plausibility based on knowledge of social organization. This is one reason he is often treated as an important precursor of sociological reasoning.
Limit
: His analysis reflects the political and economic worlds he observed; it should not be mechanically mapped onto modern nation-states without adaptation.
Positivism
: Comte argued that society could be studied systematically using methods inspired by science. He sought social laws and emphasized observation and comparison.
Law of three stages
: He proposed theological, metaphysical and positive stages of intellectual development. The scheme is historically important but highly linear and not supported as a universal empirical law.
Social statics and dynamics
: Statics concerned order and structural relations; dynamics concerned social progress and change. The distinction helped define sociology's dual concern with stability and transformation.
Legacy
: Comte helped name and institutionalize sociology, but contemporary sociology is more pluralistic methodologically and does not accept his full evolutionary philosophy.
Evolution and differentiation
: Spencer described social evolution as increasing differentiation and integration of institutions. He used organismic analogies to explain interdependence.
Military and industrial societies
: He contrasted societies organized around coercive military coordination with those organized more through voluntary exchange.
Social Darwinism caution

: Spencer's ideas later became associated with social Darwinist arguments, but simplified textbook presentations often mix his own writings with later ideological uses. Avoid turning 'survival of the fittest' into a scientific justification for inequality.
Criticism
: His evolutionary schemes were too universal and often treated social complexity as a single direction of progress.
Social facts

: Durkheim argued that social facts such as law, norms and institutions are external to individuals and exercise constraint. They should be explained by other social facts rather than reduced to individual psychology.
Division of labour
: Mechanical solidarity rests on similarity and a strong collective conscience; organic solidarity arises from specialization and interdependence in complex societies.
Anomie
: Rapid change or weak regulation can create anomie, a condition in which norms fail to regulate aspirations effectively.
Suicide
: Durkheim used variation in suicide rates to demonstrate social explanation through integration and regulation. His categories were egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic.
Religion
: He analyzed religion as a source of collective representations and solidarity, especially through ritual.
Criticism
: Durkheim sometimes treated social cohesion as more unified than modern plural societies permit, and his historical data on suicide had measurement limitations.
Historical materialism

: Marx argued that the organization of material production strongly shapes social relations and historical change. Productive forces and relations of production can develop contradictions that transform a mode of production.
Mode of production
: A mode of production combines productive forces—labour, technology and resources—with social relations governing ownership and control.
Class

: Under capitalism, Marx emphasized the bourgeoisie, who own capital, and the proletariat, who sell labour power. Intermediate classes exist, but the core conflict concerns control of production and surplus.
Surplus value and exploitation

: Workers produce value during labour, while wages do not equal the full value created. Marx analyzed profit and accumulation through this unequal relationship rather than through individual employer morality.
Alienation
: Workers can become alienated from product, process, human creative potential and other workers when labour is controlled externally and commodities dominate social relations.
Ideology
: Dominant ideas can make historically specific social relations appear natural. Later Marxists developed more complex accounts of culture and consent.
Change

: Class conflict can generate political struggle and systemic change, but historical developments did not follow Marx's predictions uniformly. Capitalism proved adaptable and class structures became more differentiated.
Contemporary relevance

: Marx remains influential for analyzing inequality, labour, commodification and concentration of capital. His framework is strongest when used analytically rather than as a prediction that every society must pass through an identical sequence.
Social action
: Weber defined sociology around meaningful social action. To explain behaviour, researchers interpret the meanings actors attach to conduct while also examining causal patterns.
Verstehen
: Interpretive understanding does not mean accepting every actor's explanation uncritically; it means reconstructing subjective meaning as part of causal analysis.
Class, status and party
: Weber treated stratification as multidimensional. Market position shapes class, social honour shapes status groups, and parties organize power.
Authority
: Traditional authority rests on custom, charismatic authority on devotion to an extraordinary leader, and legal-rational authority on impersonal rules and offices.
Bureaucracy
: Bureaucracy uses hierarchy, specialization, written rules and career offices. It is technically efficient for many tasks but can create rigidity and an 'iron cage' of rationalized control.
Religion and capitalism

: In The Protestant Ethic, Weber argued that certain religious ideas helped shape disciplined economic conduct in a particular historical setting. He did not claim religion was the sole cause of capitalism.
Rationalization
: Modern societies increasingly organize action through calculation, rules and efficiency. Rationalization expands predictability while potentially reducing substantive freedom and meaning.
Action system
: Parsons sought to explain how shared values and role expectations create stable social order despite diverse individual interests.
Pattern variables
: He developed ideal-type choices such as universalism versus particularism to compare role orientations.
AGIL
: Systems must adapt to environments, attain goals, integrate components and maintain value patterns. Parsons linked these functions with institutions such as economy, polity and family/culture.
Contribution
: His systems framework pushed sociology toward comparative institutional analysis and emphasized normative order.
Criticism
: The theory is highly abstract, difficult to test directly and often gives insufficient attention to domination, inequality and abrupt change.

blocks.text: Durkheim, Marx and Weber: a high-yield comparison

items.text: Durkheim
: Asks how social order and solidarity are maintained, using social facts and integration/regulation as key mechanisms.
Marx
: Asks how material production and class power create exploitation, conflict and historical transformation.
Weber
: Asks how meaning, authority, ideas, markets and institutions interact; he treats causation as multidimensional and historically specific.

segments.text: These thinkers are best compared around questions and mechanisms, not reduced to one-word labels such as 'order', 'conflict' and 'meaning'. All three analyzed modernity, institutions and historical change, but they selected different causal priorities.

rows: Differentiation increases interdependence but can weaken regulation
Mode of production, class, surplus value, alienation
Capital accumulation and class relations drive conflict/change
Can be reduced too narrowly to economics
Modernity expands rational calculation and bureaucracy
Complex and less reducible to one master cause

items.text: Make one page for each thinker with five boxes.
Prepare Durkheim vs Marx vs Weber as a core comparison.
Use an institution such as education and show how functionalism, interactionism and conflict theory would ask different questions.
Avoid invented quotations; paraphrase concepts unless you have verified exact wording.

rows: Avoid this error Do not force every historical thinker neatly into one of the three modern perspectives. Explain each thinker in his own intellectual context first.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define theory, explain the three perspectives, then move thinker-by-thinker with concepts and applications, ending with a comparative section.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).

• Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah; Durkheim, The Division of Labour in Society and Suicide; Marx, Capital and related writings; Weber, Economy and Society and The Protestant Ethic; Parsons, The Social System.
• Theories are lenses, not complete copies of reality.
• Functionalism emphasizes order; conflict theory emphasizes power/inequality; interactionism emphasizes meaning in everyday life.
• Durkheim, Marx and Weber differ in both method and explanation.
• Ibn Khaldun is important for early systematic analysis of social cohesion and historical change.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
